title: The history of the idli
tagline: Eleven hundred years from a black gram cake in a Kannada story to a packet of live batter in the fridge.
intro: The name idli is first written down in 920 CE, but the dish in those early texts had no rice, no overnight ferment and no steamer. Nobody knows for certain when or where the three came together, and historians still argue about it. What is certain is newer: in 1955 a Coimbatore machine took the labour out of grinding, and in 1965 scientists found the bacterium that makes the batter rise.

eras.name: Before the name
eras.summary: Black gram is grown across India and steam is used in southern kitchens. The evidence is thin, and it sits at the heart of a later argument.

eras.name: Idli in words
eras.summary: Kannada and Sanskrit texts name iddalige and iddarika, made of black gram. The word reaches Tamil, and the dish travels with the people who make it.

eras.name: Finding the invisible workers
eras.summary: Chemists find lactic acid, microbiologists find the bacteria, and food scientists in Mysuru, New York and Kolkata measure what happens in the batter.

eras.name: Machines and restaurants
eras.summary: Tiffin rooms make idli a city breakfast, a wartime shortage creates rava idli, and Coimbatore's wet grinder ends the hour at the stone.

eras.name: The origin debate
eras.summary: K. T. Achaya suggests that fermenting and steaming came from Indonesia. Others disagree, and the question stays open.

eras.name: Packets, pride and orbit
eras.summary: Fresh batter is sold chilled, the wet grinder wins a protected name, idli gets its own day and a place on a space menu.

events.title: Steam in the south Indian kitchen
events.text: The archaeologist Dorian Fuller, who studies ancient crops and cooking, holds that steaming was already in use in Neolithic south India around 2000 BCE. Black gram, the bean behind urad dal, is native to South Asia and has been grown there since ancient times.
events.why: It matters for the origin debate: if steaming is this old in the south, the method did not have to be imported later.

events.title: A traveller who saw no steamers
events.text: The Chinese monk Xuanzang travelled through India in the seventh century and wrote about what he saw. The food historian K. T. Achaya later cited him as saying that India had no steaming vessel at the time. Others doubt that one traveller's remark can settle what every Indian kitchen did.
events.why: This single report is one leg of the argument that steamed idli came from abroad.

events.title: The first written idli
events.text: A Kannada work called the Vaddaradhane mentions a food named iddalige. It is the oldest known reference to idli by name. The dish it describes was made from black gram batter alone.
events.why: The name is over a thousand years old, even if the recipe behind it has changed.

events.title: Urad soaked in buttermilk
events.text: The Kannada encyclopaedia Lokopakara gives a recipe. Black gram is soaked in buttermilk, ground to a fine paste and mixed with the clear water of curd and spices.
events.why: The buttermilk shows that cooks already wanted sourness, but took it from curd and not from an overnight ferment.

events.title: A king writes down iddarika
events.text: Someshvara III ruled from 1126 to 1138 and compiled the Manasollasa, a Sanskrit encyclopaedia of about a hundred subjects, cooking among them. It includes a recipe for iddarika. Like the earlier texts, it does not mention rice, a long fermentation or steaming.
events.why: Three early texts agree on the name, and all three leave out the three things that define a modern idli.

events.title: Itali appears in Tamil
events.text: The earliest surviving Tamil work to mention the dish, as itali, is the Maccapuranam, dated to the 17th century. By then the word had moved from Kannada into Tamil.
events.why: It marks the dish spreading across the south, though the text does not tell us when rice and steaming joined the recipe.

events.title: The acid in sour things
events.text: Scheele, a Swedish chemist who ran a pharmacy, separated a new acid from sour milk. It was later named lactic acid. The same acid gives fermented idli batter its sour taste.
events.why: Chemistry now had a name for what sourness is.

events.date: c. early 19th century, by local tradition
events.title: Weavers carry idli to Ramasseri
events.text: According to the families who make it, Mudaliar weavers from Tamil Nadu settled in Ramasseri village about two hundred years ago. When weaving declined, the women began to sell idlis. Theirs are thin and flat, steamed on cloth stretched over clay pots.
events.why: It shows how one batter turned into many local idlis as people moved.

events.title: Souring is the work of living microbes
events.text: Most chemists of the time thought fermentation was a purely chemical change. Pasteur showed that lactic acid is made by tiny living organisms as they grow.
events.why: Every later study of idli batter starts from this idea: look for the microbe.

events.title: Leuconostoc gets its name
events.who: Lev Tsenkovskii and Philippe van Tieghem
events.text: A slime-making bacterium that troubled sugar factories was described by Tsenkovskii and placed in a new genus, Leuconostoc, by van Tieghem, both in 1878. It grows best at about 30 °C and makes lactic acid, ethanol and carbon dioxide from sugar.
events.why: Nearly ninety years later the same species turned out to be what raises idli batter.

events.title: A coffee club in Bangalore
events.who: Parampalli Yagnanarayana Maiya and his brothers
events.text: The Maiya brothers opened the Brahmin Coffee Club on Lalbagh Road. In 1960 it moved and took the name Mavalli Tiffin Rooms, MTR. It became one of the best-known places in the city for idli and coffee.
events.why: Restaurants like this turned a home breakfast into a city habit.

events.title: Rava idli, born of a rice shortage
events.text: During the Second World War rice was scarce in south India. MTR says its cooks tried semolina in place of rice and made the first rava idli. It is mixed with curd and a tempering of mustard and cashew, and needs no overnight ferment.
events.why: It is the best-known case of the idli idea being rebuilt with a different grain.

events.title: A national food laboratory in Mysore
events.who: Council of Scientific and Industrial Research
events.text: The Central Food Technological Research Institute opened in the Cheluvamba palace, given by the Maharaja of Mysore. Much of the later science of idli batter, from urad gum to starter cultures, was done there.
events.why: India now had a laboratory that took everyday foods seriously.

events.title: The wet grinder is born
events.text: For centuries batter was ground by hand in a stone mortar, which took time and strength. In 1955 P. Sabapathy of Coimbatore built a motor-driven wet grinder, and later took it to Chennai and Madurai.
events.why: Grinding stopped being an hour of labour, and idli could become an everyday breakfast.

events.title: Grinders go commercial
events.text: Krishnamurthy started Lakshmi Grinders, which made the machine widely popular. Coimbatore already had foundries, motor makers and granite nearby, and a cluster of grinder workshops grew around them.
events.why: A local invention became an industry.

events.title: The microbe behind the rise is found
events.who: S. K. Mukherjee, M. N. Albury, C. S. Pederson, A. G. van Veen and K. H. Steinkraus
events.text: A team at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station followed idli batter through its ferment. They found that Leuconostoc mesenteroides did both the souring and the gas making, with Streptococcus faecalis and then Pediococcus becoming significant later. The microbes came with the grain.
events.why: They called it the first record of a food leavened by a lactic acid bacterium alone.

events.title: What fermenting changes, measured
events.text: In the British Journal of Nutrition, the two scientists compared fermented and unfermented idli and khaman. Fermentation raised the thiamine and riboflavin content and lowered the phytate content of both foods.
events.why: It put numbers on a change that cooks had only tasted. It is a measurement, not a health claim.

events.title: The grinder learns to tilt
events.text: Early grinders were heavy floor machines, and the batter had to be scooped out by hand. Doraiswamy invented the tilting wet grinder, whose drum tips over to pour. L. G. Varadaraj later introduced the table-top grinder for home kitchens.
events.why: The machine shrank from a shop floor to a kitchen counter.

events.title: Why urad holds the bubbles
events.who: N. S. Susheelamma and M. V. L. Rao
events.text: Working at CFTRI, Susheelamma and Rao studied what makes black gram batter so good at keeping gas. They traced it to two things: a surface-active globulin protein and a gum, an arabinogalactan. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Food Science.
events.why: It explained why idli needs urad dal and not just any pulse.

events.title: Fermented foods get their handbook
events.text: Steinkraus, a Cornell food scientist who had worked on the 1965 idli study, published the Handbook of Indigenous Fermented Foods. It was the first comprehensive book on the subject and gave idli and dosa a full scientific account.
events.why: Idli took its place beside tempeh, miso and sourdough in the world's science of fermentation.

events.title: Yeasts join the story
events.who: S. K. Soni and D. K. Sandhu
events.text: In a series of papers, Soni and Sandhu studied the microbes of idli and dosa batters. Along with the lactic bacteria they found yeasts, among them Saccharomyces, Debaryomyces and Trichosporon, and examined how they change the batter.
events.why: The ferment turned out to be a small community, not one species.

events.title: Did idli come from Indonesia?
events.text: In Indian Food: A Historical Companion, the food scientist and historian K. T. Achaya noted that the early Indian recipes lack rice, fermenting and steaming. He suggested that the modern method may have arrived between 800 and 1200 CE from Indonesia, then ruled by Hindu kings and long used to fermented foods. It was offered as a suggestion, and it is still debated. Others answer that steaming is very old in south India, or point to Arab traders on the coast, a view press reports attribute to the historian Lizzie Collingham.
events.why: It opened the most famous argument in Indian food history, and nobody has closed it.

events.title: Batter in a packet
events.who: P. C. Musthafa and his cousins
events.text: Musthafa and four cousins began grinding batter in a tiny kitchen with two grinders, a mixer and a sealing machine, and supplied a few packets a day to about 20 shops under the name iD. By 2016 the company reported making around 50,000 kg of batter a day.
events.why: Fresh, live batter became something a city home could buy, as long as it stayed cold.

events.title: Coimbatore Wet Grinder becomes a protected name
events.who: Government of Tamil Nadu and the Geographical Indications Registry
events.text: Tamil Nadu applied in 2005, and from March 2006 Coimbatore Wet Grinder has been a registered geographical indication. As of 2015 the city had more than 700 makers, producing about 75,000 of every 100,000 grinders made in India each month.
events.why: A kitchen machine joined Darjeeling tea on the list of things tied to a place.

events.title: Chosen cultures for packed batter
events.who: J. Sridevi, P. M. Halami and S. V. N. Vijayendra
events.text: CFTRI scientists tested selected lactic bacteria and yeasts as starters for idli batter and followed the batter in storage. Fresh batter began at pH 6.7, and counts of lactic bacteria and yeasts reached about a billion per gram and more.
events.why: It was part of the effort to make packed batter rise the same way every time.

events.title: The rise, measured hour by hour
events.text: Two food technologists tracked batters of 2 : 1, 3 : 1 and 4 : 1 rice to dal for 22 hours at 20 to 26 °C. The batter grew to between 1.62 and 3.2 times its volume, the pH fell from 5.9 to about 4.2 and the acidity rose from 0.44 to 0.91 per cent.
events.why: These are the numbers the simulator in this box is fitted to.

events.title: World Idli Day
events.text: Eniyavan, a Chennai idli caterer, began marking 30 March as World Idli Day. It has been picked up by restaurants, newspapers and delivery apps every year since.
events.why: A breakfast got its own day on the calendar.

events.title: New food tables for India
events.who: T. Longvah and colleagues, ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition
events.text: The National Institute of Nutrition published the Indian Food Composition Tables 2017, with 151 components measured in 528 key foods sampled across the country, parboiled rice and black gram dal among them.
events.why: It is the standard source for what Indian grains hold.

events.title: Idli on a space menu
events.text: For the Gaganyaan crewed mission, the Defence Food Research Laboratory prepared a menu of Indian dishes adapted from its packed rations. Reports listed idli among them, with upma, pulao and halwa.
events.why: The thousand-year-old dish was packed for orbit.

facts: The oldest idli recipes, from 920 to 1130 CE, use black gram only. They mention no rice, no overnight ferment and no steaming.
Idli batter is raised by a bacterium, not a yeast. In 1965 scientists called it the first known food leavened by a lactic acid bacterium alone.
Nobody adds the bacteria. They arrive on the grains, mostly the urad dal.
As of 2015, about three of every four wet grinders made in India each month came from Coimbatore.
Rava idli is traced by MTR of Bengaluru to a rice shortage during the Second World War.
